findings.title: Negative-offset slicing on a Django QuerySet raises an error / is unsupported
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result intentionally allows `cursor.offset < 0` when `enable_advanced_features` is set, slicing with `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset is negative. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing: `QuerySet[-5:...]` raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'). The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is simply wrong, so this 'advanced' path will crash (or, for sequence-like backends, silently return semantically wrong rows) whenever a client sends a cursor with a negative offset. Since Cursor.from_string accepts any int from the client-supplied cursor string, any authorized user of the audit logs endpoint can trigger this by hand-crafting a cursor.

findings.title: Undocumented, untested query-parameter-driven paginator switch on a public endpoint
findings.body: The endpoint now branches on an undocumented `optimized_pagination=true` request parameter and a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with an `enable_advanced_features` flag. This changes pagination behavior for API consumers (cursor format/semantics, result boundaries) based on a hidden flag, has no test coverage anywhere in the diff, and is not mentioned in API docs. The 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' justification in paginator.py is also misleading: the flag gates behavior, not authorization, and the paginator change itself is the risky part. Either remove this path or add tests and document the parameter.

findings.title: zpopmin eviction silently drops span payloads, including possibly the root span
findings.body: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, the script calls `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, permanently deleting span payloads from the buffer. The evicted spans (those with the earliest end timestamps — which typically includes the root/segment span, since it starts first) are never flushed to the buffered-spans topic; they are silently lost with no metric or log. The previous behavior (skipping oversized segments with an error log and a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric) at least made the loss observable. Additionally, evicting the root span while still setting the `span-buf:hrs:` key means the flushed segment will have `has_root_span` set but no span with `is_segment: true`, producing malformed segments downstream.

findings.title: Hardcoded eviction limit of 1000 conflicts with configurable max_segment_spans=1001
findings.body: The eviction threshold is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua, while SpansBuffer still exposes `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` as a constructor parameter (now unused after the Python-side span-count check was removed from _load_segment_data). The off-by-one mismatch and the dead configuration parameter mean operators who tune `max_segment_spans` (e.g. via options) will have no effect, and the previously-enforced byte-size-only limit no longer matches the documented behavior. The limit should be passed as an ARGV so it stays configurable, or the stale parameter removed.

findings.title: Redirect-follow loop limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000
findings.body: The redirect resolution loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations with no explanation and the explanatory comment removed. For traces whose redirect chains exceed depth 1000, the loop exits without resolving to the final set key; the script then writes `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` with a non-final `set_span_id`, permanently corrupting the redirect map and causing the trace's spans to be split across multiple segments (data fragmentation) with no error or metric. If the reduction was intentional (e.g. Lua execution time), the failure mode should at least be detectable, and the redirect_depth metric already returned makes the old limit observable — reducing it silently is a behavioral regression.

findings.title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead after removing the span-count check in _load_segment_data
findings.body: _load_segment_data no longer enforces `max_segment_spans` (the check and its `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric were deleted in favor of Lua-side eviction), but the constructor still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans=1001`. This is misleading configuration: changing it has no effect, and the docstring/comment contract ('Segments exceeding a certain size are skipped') is now only true for byte size. Remove the parameter or wire it into the Lua script.
